passage: Note from the team lead, Thursday. I am Zainab. In the design meeting, Aditi cleared her throat sharply twice while Manav presented, and the room went stiff. Some thought she disagreed and Manav looked worried. I thought it could also be a tickle. I decided not to guess, so at the end I said, "Aditi, is there anything you would like to say on that?" She said she had a dry throat and had been meaning to mention a small point about the colour palette. Manav laughed with relief. I noted that a throat-clear is a weak cue and that a simple follow-up question worked well. I will encourage direct follow-ups.

qa.q: What did Aditi mention at the end?
qa.a: She mentioned a small point about the colour palette.

qa.q: What did Manav think when Aditi cleared her throat, and what was the truth?
qa.a: Manav looked worried, as if it meant disagreement. The truth was that Aditi had a dry throat and a small point to add.

qa.q: What worked in Zainab's approach?
qa.a: Zainab asked, "Aditi, is there anything you would like to say on that?" instead of guessing at the meaning.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt when the room went stiff?
qa.a: Aditi may have been unaware or embarrassed, since a dry throat was all it was.

grounding: Team lead's note on a throat-clear that colleagues read as disagreement, resolved by a simple follow-up question.

passage: Wed, 8 pm. In today's client call, Shreya grunted when Manjula said the launch might slip. I am Manjula, and my chest tightened. Did the grunt mean she disagreed? Was she annoyed? I wanted to ask but felt shy. During the second half, Shreya cleared her throat again while I talked and I lost my place. After the call I sent a message: "Is there a point you would like to raise about the launch date?" Shreya replied, "Sorry, I have a cold and was clearing my throat. But yes, I had one thought." We spoke for five minutes. I need to remember these sounds are weak cues. Asking is fairer than guessing.

qa.q: What did Shreya say she had?
qa.a: Shreya said she had a cold.

qa.q: What did Manjula think when Shreya grunted, and what was going on?
qa.a: Manjula's chest tightened as if the grunt might mean disagreement or annoyance. In fact Shreya had a cold and one thought to add.

qa.q: What did Manjula do that helped?
qa.a: Manjula sent a message asking whether Shreya had a point to raise about the launch date.

qa.q: How might Shreya have seen the exchange?
qa.a: Shreya probably had no idea the throat sounds had worried Manjula, and was glad of the chance to share the thought.

grounding: Diary entry about a throat-clear or grunt read as possible disagreement, resolved by a follow-up question.

passage: At the gram sabha under the school's tin roof in Nandurbar district, Varun was explaining the plan for the new drainage line along the main lane. Halfway through, Lavanya, the ASHA worker in the front row, gave a short grunt. Varun faltered. Was she against it? He'd been warned that some families didn't want digging near their doors. He paused and turned to her. "Lavanya-tai, anything you wanted to say?" She waved a hand, coughing. "No, no, dust in my throat. Carry on." A few people chuckled. Varun smiled and went on. Near the end, old Bhikaji at the back cleared his throat loudly and folded his arms. This time Varun didn't assume either way. "Bhikaji-kaka, anything from your side?" The old man frowned. "Yes. The line goes right past my well." Varun pulled out the map. "Show me."

qa.q: What was Varun explaining?
qa.a: The plan for the new drainage line along the main lane.

qa.q: What did Varun fear Lavanya's grunt meant?
qa.a: Varun felt a flicker of worry that she was against the plan, since he'd been warned some families didn't want digging near their doors.

qa.q: Why was asking a follow-up question the right move both times?
qa.a: The cues were weak: Lavanya's grunt was just dust, but Bhikaji's throat-clearing hid a real concern about his well, which came out only because Varun asked.

qa.q: How might Bhikaji have felt being asked directly?
qa.a: Bhikaji likely felt taken seriously and able to raise his worry about the well, rather than grumbling silently at the back.

grounding: Shows a young professional unsure whether a grunt or throat-clear signals disagreement and fairly asking each person if they wanted to add something.

passage: Rosa was halfway through her first results presentation at the lab in Seville when Dr. Elif Aydın grunted: a short, low "hmph" from the back row. Rosa's mouth went dry. Was the data wrong? She clicked to the next slide. Another grunt, then a throat-clear. Her palms started to sweat. She could keep going and hope, or she could ask. She stopped. "Dr. Aydın, is there something on this slide you'd like to raise?" Elif blinked, then smiled. "No, no. Sorry. I grunt when I'm thinking. A bad habit. Actually, I was thinking this curve is very clean." A couple of postdocs laughed; clearly this was well known. "Oh," Rosa said, relieved. "Good. I'll keep going." Afterwards one of the postdocs whispered to her, "Her grunts scared all of us in our first year too."

qa.q: What did Elif say she was thinking about the curve?
qa.a: That the curve is very clean.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling when Elif grunted?
qa.a: Rosa felt anxious, mouth dry and palms sweating, fearing the grunts meant the data was wrong.

qa.q: Why was stopping to ask a good choice?
qa.a: A grunt is a weak cue, and asking whether Elif had something to raise replaced a scary guess with the real meaning, letting Rosa continue relieved.

qa.q: How had the postdocs experienced Elif's grunts?
qa.a: They had been scared by them in their first year too, which is why they laughed knowingly.

grounding: Shows a young professional reading a senior's grunts as disagreement and asking a fair follow-up that reveals a thinking habit.

passage:
In the fourth-floor conference room at the water board office, Lokesh was halfway through the new pipe-inspection schedule when Naveen cleared his throat. Loudly. A minute later came a short grunt.
Lokesh's mind raced. Was Naveen disagreeing? Naveen had built the old schedule; maybe he hated this one. Or maybe it was just the dusty AC. Two sounds, no words: not much to go on.
Lokesh paused at the next slide and turned to him. "Naveen, is there something you'd like to add?"
Naveen looked surprised, then nodded slowly. "Actually, yes. Ward 7 floods in July. Your schedule sends the team there in the second week."
"I didn't know that. Good catch."
He moved Ward 7 to June on the spot. After the meeting, Naveen stopped at his desk. "Thanks for asking. I wasn't going to interrupt."

qa.q: Which ward floods in July?
qa.a: Ward 7 floods in July.

qa.q: What was Lokesh worried about when Naveen cleared his throat?
qa.a: Lokesh worried that Naveen disagreed with the new schedule, having built the old one, though it could simply have been the dusty AC.

qa.q: What made Lokesh's question a good move?
qa.a: It was a simple, open invitation that accused no one, so Naveen could share the flood problem he wasn't going to interrupt with. 👍

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about being asked?
qa.a: Naveen felt grateful and a little surprised, since he had held back to avoid interrupting.

grounding: A throat-clear or grunt in a meeting is a weak cue, so asking whether the person wants to add something is fair.
